audience.programmeDescription: Leiden’s broad Ancient Near Eastern Studies route examines ancient Egypt, the Near East, Greece and Rome through history, religion, archaeology, material culture and written sources. It provides orientation in languages and writing systems alongside museum and heritage study. Specialist ancient-language training belongs to the other tracks.
audience.comparisonExplanation: This comparison assesses the documented 90 EC historical, material, textual and heritage core of Leiden’s broad route. UCR can combine ancient archaeology, Athenian society, comparative empires, ancient literature and museum/heritage inquiry in a broader programme. Near Eastern historical depth, language and script history, regional religions and papyrology remain differences. The 10 EC history choice, 10 EC Roman North Africa seminar, 15 EC final work and unidentified 25 EC are excluded from the academic comparison. Genuine 30 EC open study is shown separately; complete degree progression is not certified.

curriculum.limitation: Documented content totals 155 of the nominal 180 EC. Only the specified 90 EC subject and method core is assessed. The 35 EC of documented choice, Roman seminar and final work remain unassessed; the unidentified 25 required EC and full entry/progression remain unresolved. Philosophy counts once for 5 EC, with its year placement unconfirmed. The separate genuine 30 EC open space has no assumed contents.

componentNotes.ono04: Counted once for 5 EC. The curriculum lists two versions of the same core course; its correct year allocation remains under review.
componentNotes.ono05: Successful completion is part of the first-year study-advice requirements, together with Written Sources of the Ancient Near East and the language panorama. This is a 10 EC seminar, not extra credit for each repeated reference.
componentNotes.ono06: Successful completion forms part of the route’s first-year study-advice requirements.
componentNotes.ono08: Successful completion forms part of the route’s first-year study-advice requirements.
componentNotes.ono18: Entry requires successful completion of Ancient History and meeting the study-advice threshold.
componentNotes.ono19: One of two approved 10 EC second-year choices. Entry for this route requires Ancient History and the first-year Ancient Near Eastern Studies seminar. Confirmation is still needed that the current seminar meets the applicable thematic-seminar requirement for this cohort.
componentNotes.ono20: The 5 EC thesis seminar requires completion of the first two bachelor years. An exception requires consultation with the study adviser and examination-board permission. Its work supports the separate 10 EC thesis.
componentNotes.ono21: Entry is stated for students who completed the History first year and both second-year History seminars, including one in the same field. Greek and Latin Language and Culture students are also eligible. Ordinary entry from this Ancient Near Eastern Studies route remains unconfirmed.
componentNotes.ono22: The 10 EC thesis requires completion of the first two bachelor years and participation in the thesis seminar. The topic and research approach are agreed with the supervisor, whose appointment requires examination-board approval. The thesis has a maximum of 10,000 words, including footnotes and excluding the bibliography and appendices. Full year-one and year-two completion remains dependent on the curriculum repair.
componentNotes.ono23: 30 EC in the first semester of year three for a minor, approved courses, an approved internship or study abroad. An individual course package needs approval and normally permits at most 10 EC at level 100 and requires at least 10 EC at level 300 or above. Courses must avoid overlap with compulsory study; Honours College courses cannot count. Recognized full 30 EC minors at Leiden, Delft or Erasmus generally need no separate approval. An internship requires prior approval; a placement or study-abroad place is not guaranteed.

core: Ancient societies, material culture and historical power
Myth, written sources, language and cultural meaning

Historical, textual, material, digital and qualitative inquiry

trace: Actual R-based cleaning, joining, visualization and textual/spatial data analysis supplies an identifiable digital-humanities research function. No ancient corpus or full AI/platform teaching assumed.

Actual grammar, discourse, modality, ideology and stylistic interpretation supports the core inquiry into language, texts and identity. It is not historical Semitic linguistics or ancient-language proficiency.

candidates.label: Ancient-language and textual scholarship
candidates.reason: The three specialist fields were each assessed on their own actual language/script/corpus requirements. Their common philological question is a coherent candidate, not an arbitrary residual group. UCR stylistics, comparative myth and literature provide real analysis, but additional general cognitive, creative or communication courses do not establish a sustained specialist ancient textual programme. This is a subject/method limitation, not a language-only veto on the already broader route. Do not manufacture a schedule or arbitrary four-course substitutions.

selection.assessment: Stop at one after that candidate fails. Museum/heritage, material-culture and reception directions are already substantive parts of the closest curriculum; relabeling the same courses is not another educational choice. No third slot is constructed after failure.

alternatives.label: Ancient societies and cultural heritage
alternatives.concept: Study ancient societies through material objects, historical power, myth and written-source interpretation, then examine how museums, collecting and heritage shape their later meanings. Sustained world and Greek archaeology, Athenian democracy, comparative empires, ancient literature and critical heritage inquiry anchor the programme. Visual, textual, digital and qualitative research deepen those questions. The programme responds to the documented broad academic core; it does not reproduce specialist Near Eastern chronology, languages, religious institutions or final research.
alternatives.labelReason: Names sustained ancient material/textual/historical inquiry and the actual museum/heritage strand; no specialist UCR track, Near Eastern survey or complete degree equivalence claimed.
progression: Foundation visual/textual and material methods precede advanced Greek heritage, museum, historiographic and interpretive projects where feasible. Actual open-curriculum formal rules govern, with no invented disciplinary prerequisites.

notes.text: This comparison assesses the documented 90 EC historical, material, textual and heritage core. UCR offers a broader ancient-societies and cultural-heritage programme. Regional depth, language and script history, papyrology and ancient religious institutions remain differences. Required choices, final research and a complete valid external degree pathway are not assessed. Optional independent research is additional to UCR’s scheduled 180 EC.

blocks: Ancient societies, material and textual inquiry
Ancient Persian and Roman imperial histories and source-based comparison address an identifiable ancient imperial-power part; not the full Egypt/Mesopotamia chronology.
Both explicitly teach artefact observation, technical drawing, cataloguing and interpretation. UCR studies ancient craft/material evidence across regions; the Egyptian/RMO corpus remains distinct.

Both examine Athenian political life through historical sources and material culture. UCR gives sustained citizenship, myth/religion and archaeological analysis; Leiden’s broader Roman and late-antique survey differs.
Actual textual/spatial data cleaning, analysis and visualization addresses an identifiable data-method part of digital humanities; not full AI/platform theory.
Both substantively examine colonial collecting, restitution, ownership and museum display. UCR’s West African art is not an Egypt/Near East survey.
Both analyze museum presentation and curatorial choices. UCR teaches modern/global art institutions; ancient RMO collections and object-care practices remain different.

Both explicitly teach question formation, critical source work and a substantial research paper. This is a specific research function; UCR uses American historical inquiry, not a guaranteed Near Eastern topic or supervisor.
The dedicated regional subject or source method is not reproduced by a directly adequate UCR component; broader related interpretation remains a programme contribution, not a forced row match.
Philosophy of science and humanities epistemology remain distinct; general ethical/interpretive methods do not reproduce this core, whose year allocation is unconfirmed.

acceptance.claim: One complete feasible UCR programme meaningfully responds to the documented 90 EC historical, material, textual and heritage core through sustained ancient archaeology, Athenian civic and religious culture, comparative empires, ancient literary interpretation, museum/ownership inquiry and concrete research methods. Near Eastern chronology, script/language history, regional religions and papyrology remain important gaps. The comparison does not assess the restricted/advanced seminars, final research, missing required 25 EC or complete external degree eligibility.
acceptance.targetContext: Leiden BA Ancient Near Eastern Studies, neutral broad The Ancient Near Eastern World route, current 2026–2027. Assessed 90 EC core; 155 documented EC displayed, including 35 unassessed choice/advanced/final EC and separate genuine 30 open. Missing required 25 EC not invented.
acceptance.challengeMethod: Separately identified same-AI source-first final pass reading underlying official and current UCR evidence, then challenging exact finished inputs. No independent human or separate agent.
